item.title: Retired Police Officer recounts emotional wait as missing daughter is found safe
item.description: Timoci Lutunauga, the father of Maca Lutunauga, a Health Inspector with the Ministry of Health who was among the group reported missing at sea, struggled to hold back his emotions as he recounted the family's ordeal. While speaking to fijivillage News, the retired police officer says he had never cried in his life, but was devastated when he received a call informing him that his eldest daughter w
item.content:encoded:
Timoci Lutunauga, the father of Maca Lutunauga, a Health Inspector with the Ministry of Health who was among the group reported missing at sea, struggled to hold back his emotions as he recounted the family's ordeal.

While speaking to fijivillage News, the retired police officer says he had never cried in his life, but was devastated when he received a call informing him that his eldest daughter was drifting at sea.

He says he was unable to sleep or eat for the past 48 hours.

Lutunauga shared that he told his family he could not bring himself to eat while knowing his daughter was out at sea without food.

Drawing on his experience as a former police officer who had travelled extensively, including throughout the Lau Group, he says he understood just how harsh and cold conditions at sea could be.

Throughout the ordeal, the father of two kept his family united through daily devotions, praying constantly for the safety of those missing.

When news finally came that the group had been found, he said he could no longer contain his emotions and gave thanks to God for His mercy and love.

Lutunauga also expressed his heartfelt gratitude to the people of Lau, who used their own boats and resources to assist in the search, as well as the Fiji Navy and all other agencies including the Lomaiviti Princess 12 crew and individuals involved in the rescue efforts.

Timoci Lutunauga lives with his wife and their two daughters.

item.title: Sanday reveals Flying Fijians players sought $1,000 daily allowance, but Fiji Rugby could not afford it - Sanday
item.description: Fiji Rugby Chair John Sanday says the FIJI Water Flying Fijians players had asked for an increase in allowance from $500 a day to $1,000 per day during their Nations Championship Tour in Europe. In an interview with fijivillage Play With Alipate Narawa, Sanday stated that this is a normal employer and employee situation that the players were requesting and some of that the FRU was able to deliver
item.content:encoded:
Fiji Rugby Chair John Sanday says the FIJI Water Flying Fijians players had asked for an increase in allowance from $500 a day to $1,000 per day during their Nations Championship Tour in Europe.

In an interview with fijivillage Play With Alipate Narawa, Sanday stated that this is a normal employer and employee situation that the players were requesting and some of that the FRU was able to deliver like Business Class seats for the players.

He says on the payment side, they were not able to deliver on the $1,000 a day because they are not in a financial position, and they are talking about a 40 man squad.

The FRU Chair says some of them have been working on the Board for 2 years, and they have given their 100 percent but have not been paid a cent.

He says it is a conversation, adding that if they had won, then they would have been paid.

When queried on this not being the first time that players have held the FRU hostage based on pay, Sanday says it is the first time for him, although he knows it has happened several times before.

Sanday says it is not something he likes to entertain.

He says if the team performs, then they will be happy to pay them.

You can watch the full interview on fijivillage Play at 8pm on our facebook page, YouTube and TikTok accounts, fijivillage.

item.title: 10-month-old baby youngest of 64 children supported by WOWS Kids Fiji
item.description: A 10-month-old baby is the youngest of the 64 children currently receiving support from WOWS Kids Fiji, highlighting the need for parents to recognise the early signs of childhood cancer. Speaking at the launch of Childhood Cancer Awareness Month 2026, WOWS Kids Fiji board member Anabel Ali says the organisation is currently caring for 64 children battling cancer across Fiji, including 43 boys and
item.content:encoded:
A 10-month-old baby is the youngest of the 64 children currently receiving support from WOWS Kids Fiji, highlighting the need for parents to recognise the early signs of childhood cancer.

Speaking at the launch of Childhood Cancer Awareness Month 2026, WOWS Kids Fiji board member Anabel Ali says the organisation is currently caring for 64 children battling cancer across Fiji, including 43 boys and 21 girls.

Ali says WOWS Kids Fiji has lost five children since January this year and sees around 30 new childhood cancer cases annually.

She says the number of children affected by childhood cancer could be higher, as some cases may be managed directly through hospitals or private institutions.

She says the focus of Childhood Cancer Awareness Month is to educate parents, caregivers, teachers, and communities about the early warning signs of childhood cancer and the importance of seeking medical attention early.

INSERT: Ali on early detection 30th July

Ali says Fiji launches Childhood Cancer Awareness Month in August, a month ahead of the global campaign in September, to give more people an opportunity to learn about the warning signs of childhood cancer and the importance of early diagnosis and treatment.

She says WOWS Kids Fiji is not a medical organisation but works alongside health professionals to ensure children and their families receive the support they need throughout treatment.

She says the organisation assists families with transport, medical supplies when hospitals are unable to provide them, nutritional support, counselling, educational assistance, and private tutoring for children who are away from school during treatment.

Ali says the organisation also supports caregivers, an aspect that is often overlooked, through food assistance, counselling, laundry services, and opportunities for self-care.

She stresses that early detection can make a difference, noting that some children have recovered after receiving timely treatment.

She is urging parents and communities to pay attention to changes in children and seek medical advice as soon as concerns arise.

item.title: Children with disabilities help shape Fiji's first national rights study
item.description: The Fiji Human Rights and Anti-Discrimination Commission launched the country's first national baseline study on the rights of children with disabilities, drawing on the experiences of children, their parents and caregivers to help guide future policies and services. Speaking at the launch, Acting Permanent Secretary for the Ministry of Women, Children and Social Protection Selina Kuruleca says th
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Human Rights and Anti-Discrimination Commission launched the country's first national baseline study on the rights of children with disabilities, drawing on the experiences of children, their parents and caregivers to help guide future policies and services.

Speaking at the launch, Acting Permanent Secretary for the Ministry of Women, Children and Social Protection Selina Kuruleca says the report is about recognising children whose voices have too often gone unheard.

She says children with disabilities continue to face barriers such as inaccessible schools, limited transport, health services, stigma and discrimination, preventing them from participating fully in everyday life.

Kuruleca says the report goes beyond statistics because it captures the real stories of children and their families, giving the Government a better understanding of the challenges they face and helping shape policies and services that respond to their needs.

She says the findings will also help guide Fiji's National Action Plan to End Violence Against Children, ensuring children with disabilities are not left behind.

Human Rights Commissioner Veena Singh says while Fiji has made progress through legislation and awareness programmes, many children with disabilities still struggle to access education, healthcare and other essential services.

She says the report contains 24 recommendations covering education, health, social protection and justice, providing a roadmap to improve the lives of children with disabilities.

Singh also highlighted that the report has been translated into iTaukei, Hindi and Braille to ensure it is accessible to more people.

United Nations Pacific Regional Representative Heike Alefsen says the study should be used as a tool for action rather than becoming just another report, stressing that every child deserves the opportunity to participate fully in society.

Australian Government Counsellor for Human Development Emeline Cammack says the study reinforces the importance of ensuring children with disabilities can access education, healthcare and community life so they can reach their full potential.

item.title: No Fijians in Japan affected as earthquake kills 28
item.description: At least 28 people have lost their lives and thousands have been displaced after a powerful earthquake struck southwestern Japan, while the Fiji Government says there have been no reports of any Fijians being directly affected. As search and rescue efforts continue, the Fiji Government has extended its deepest condolences to the Government and people of Japan.
item.content:encoded:
At least 28 people have lost their lives and thousands have been displaced after a powerful earthquake struck southwestern Japan, while the Fiji Government says there have been no reports of any Fijians being directly affected.

As search and rescue efforts continue, the Fiji Government has extended its deepest condolences to the Government and people of Japan.

The magnitude 6.8 earthquake struck Kumamoto Prefecture on Kyushu Island on Tuesday, destroying homes, damaging power lines and causing part of a shopping centre to collapse.

An explosion at the shopping centre about an hour later claimed more lives.

Around 9,000 people are sheltering in evacuation centres, while more than 30,000 households remain without electricity.

Minister for Foreign Affairs Sakiasi Ditoka says Fiji stands in solidarity with Japan during this difficult time. The Fiji Embassy in Tokyo says there have been no reports of any Fijian nationals being directly affected by the earthquake and that it continues to monitor the situation closely.

Ditoka says Fiji's thoughts and prayers are with the families who have lost loved ones, those who have been injured, and the communities affected by the disaster.
